title: I Took the Bocce-Court Timer to the Chair Who Camped Our Numbered Palino

parts.text: I stepped into court one at 4:04 p.m. and chair Dino was already using our numbered palino. The board said: ONE COURT. NINETY MINUTES. PALINO STAYS WITH THE BOOKING. I was forty-one, league secretary, holding a clipboard that listed our match. Dino shrugged. "Chairs are the court." I photographed the board, the booking, and his roll on our pallino line. Then I asked for the court timer. At 4:12 the park desk pinged why Dino's name was on our palino. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The park desk can see Dino's roll on court one during our match.

social.video_title: He camped our numbered palino — Part 1/2
social.description: Bocce court, a chair on our pallino line, a ninety-minute clock he posted. I logged the roll. Would you have asked for the court timer?

parts.text: Dino called it warm-up rolls until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the pallino still. The palino went back to our numbered bag. Dino ran a slot of their own and told the next chair atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: CHAIRS ARE NOT THE COURT. I keep our match on a labeled tag. Dino brown-bags his rolls. The court finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Chairs are not the court — Part 2/2
social.description: Court timer, numbered palino, and a second line on the board. Were warm-up rolls ever our match?
